solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: One lies but fails to be devious (8)

indicatorNotes.devious: a devious route twists about, so the letters are rearranged

annotation.surface: A liar who can't quite manage the deceit.
annotation.walkthrough: "But fails" reads as the story of a hopeless liar; it is just the eight letters to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: A fabulist tells fables: someone who lies.

entries.clue: He barks loud words at wedding (4)

blocks.note: "I do", the words spoken at a wedding

annotation.surface: Someone shouting at a wedding.
annotation.walkthrough: "He barks" sounds like a shouting guest, but Fido is the stock name for a dog.
annotation.definitionFit: Fido is the traditional name for a pet dog, and a dog barks.

entries.clue: Psalm a bit absurd at christening (9)

annotation.definitionNote: BAPTISMAL is an adjective; 'at christening' works as one, as in 'baptismal vows' = vows at christening

indicatorNotes.absurd: an absurd arrangement is a nonsensical one, so the letters are jumbled

annotation.surface: A psalm sung at a christening that seems a little silly.
annotation.walkthrough: "A bit absurd" reads as "slightly absurd", but "a bit" belongs to the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: Baptismal means belonging to a baptism, which is a christening.

entries.clue: Being posh, did I get pulses raised? (3-2-3)

indicatorNotes.raised: in a down clue, lifting the letters up writes them bottom to top

blocks.note: dhal is a dish of lentils, which are pulses

annotation.surface: Someone putting on airs and wondering whether they set hearts racing.
annotation.walkthrough: "Pulses raised" suggests excitement; here pulses are lentils and "raised" turns the whole question "Had I dhal?" upside down.
annotation.definitionFit: Lah-di-dah describes pretentious, affected poshness.

indicatorNotes.sort of: to sort letters is to rearrange them

annotation.surface: A critic dismissing a singer's operatic manner as trite.
annotation.walkthrough: "Sort of" reads as "a kind of", but it tells you to sort the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Stereotypical means conventional and unoriginal, which is banal.

indicatorNotes.rejected: rejected things are turned back, so SO is written backwards

blocks.note: Iris, Greek goddess of the rainbow

annotation.surface: A god who has been spurned by a goddess.
annotation.walkthrough: "Rejected" looks like a rejected suitor, but it only turns SO around.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Egyptian ruler of the underworld is one god among many.

indicatorNotes.in: the maiden is literally 'in' the fiction, as a character sits in a story, so her letter goes inside it

blocks.note: m = maiden, a cricket over with no runs

annotation.surface: An ardent young heroine in a novel.
annotation.walkthrough: M for maiden is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for an over with no runs scored.
annotation.definitionFit: A stormy relationship or temper is a passionate, turbulent one.

indicatorNotes.discussed: a discussed word is spoken, so we want the sound

annotation.surface: A writer being talked about while working as a waiter in India.
annotation.walkthrough: "Serving" looks like a verb about the author; it is a noun, a portion of food.
annotation.definitionFit: Raita is a yogurt side dish served with Indian meals.

blocks.note: a billy is a male goat

annotation.surface: A donkey that has dazed a goat.
annotation.walkthrough: Every word looks like a farm animal story; "Ass" is a fool, not a donkey.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in its informal sense: both name a fool, the second as a mild, affectionate British reproach.

blocks.note: dept = department, a unit of an organisation
horse is slang for heroin, abbreviated H

annotation.surface: A unit of measure used for horses, like hands.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface suggests hands, the unit for measuring a horse; "horse" is heroin, H.
annotation.definitionFit: Depth is a measurement of how deep something is.

entries.clue: Leader’s hideout, old and current, in retreat (9)

indicatorNotes.in retreat: retreating means going backwards, so the letters run in reverse

blocks.note: an animal's lair is its hideout

annotation.surface: A leader's old hideaway, now used again, while the army falls back.
annotation.walkthrough: "Leader" looks like a general or boss; in newspapers a leader is the editorial column.
annotation.definitionFit: A leader, or leading article, is a newspaper's editorial.

blocks.note: the surface asks about cloth or stuff; the setter means 'of importance', the quality this answer lacks
'so' can stand for 'as a result', so something that is not so has no result following from it

annotation.surface: A sceptic doubting whether something really matters.
annotation.walkthrough: "So" can mean "in consequence", so something that is "not so" is IN-CONSEQUENCE; and material means important, which this is not.
annotation.definitionFit: Inconsequence is unimportance, or illogic: something that is neither material nor follows on.

blocks.note: a firm whose owners' liability is capped
read literally: a host with few guests keeps restricted society

annotation.surface: A firm that hardly ever had anyone call in.
annotation.walkthrough: The second half is read literally: a place that welcomed few visitors kept only a small circle about it.
annotation.definitionFit: The business sense is a firm whose shareholders' liability is limited; the whimsical sense is company (guests) kept to a minimum.

blocks.note: scraps and tiffs are both small quarrels

annotation.surface: People who might describe leftover food as tasteless.
annotation.walkthrough: "Scraps" looks like leftover food; it means fights.
annotation.definitionFit: A legal sense: those who bring a lawsuit are claimants, the people who may claim damages.

indicatorNotes.taking: LAMB takes A STING alongside it

blocks.note: a sting is a bite, as from an insect

annotation.surface: Someone tasting the joint as it cooks.
annotation.walkthrough: "Roasting" sits beside meat, so it looks like cooking; it means a severe telling-off.
annotation.definitionFit: Roasting and lambasting both mean criticising someone harshly.

indicatorNotes.Reportedly: what is reported is heard, so we want the sound

annotation.surface: A humble deity, so they say.
annotation.walkthrough: Loki is the Norse trickster god.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Norse trickster is one of many gods.

indicatorNotes.opening: the 1 opens up ORDNANCE by going inside it

annotation.surface: The first rule of weapon handling.
annotation.walkthrough: ORDNANCE and ORDINANCE differ by one letter, and the numeral 1 supplies it.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a decree issued by an authority, such as a local by-law, is a rule.

blocks.note: to tempt someone is to provoke them into acting

annotation.surface: A cheat whose behaviour invites disdain.
annotation.walkthrough: "Cheat to provoke" reads as one purpose clause; it is two verbs set side by side.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the feeling that someone is beneath you, shown as disdain or derision.

entries.clue: Comic actor welcomed by David Letterman (4)

indicatorNotes.welcomed by: David Letterman takes the answer in, holding it inside his name

blocks.note: the US talk-show host; the letters run across the join of his two names

annotation.surface: A comedian appearing as a guest on a US chat show.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is exactly a talk-show booking, which hides that the guest sits inside the host's name: daviD LEtterman. Eric Idle was a member of Monty Python.
annotation.definitionFit: Eric Idle is a comic actor from Monty Python.

entries.clue: Potty lid or shape that’s nearly round (10)

indicatorNotes.Potty: potty means crazy, so the letters go wild

annotation.surface: A chamber pot's lid, or its roundish outline.
annotation.walkthrough: "Potty" looks like a chamber pot beside "lid"; it means crazy.
annotation.definitionFit: Spheroidal means shaped like a spheroid, almost but not quite a sphere.

blocks.note: a bolt is a long roll of cloth, so a supply of them is textile stock
the structure of a building: its walls, roof and framework

annotation.surface: Stocking up on nuts and bolts for a building project.
annotation.walkthrough: "Bolts" looks like metal fixings; a bolt is also a roll of cloth.
annotation.definitionFit: Cloth comes in bolts, and the fabric of a building is its structure.

blocks.note: the surface pushes a schoolteacher; form is also a racehorse's record of results, and the master of it sets the odds
Windsor has a racecourse, and 'perhaps' flags it as one example among many tracks

annotation.surface: A schoolteacher at a school near Windsor, such as Eton.
annotation.walkthrough: "Form master" suggests a teacher, but form is a racehorse's record and Windsor has a racecourse. A turf accountant is a British euphemism for a bookmaker.
annotation.definitionFit: A turf accountant (bookmaker) is expert at a horse's form, and might work at Windsor races.

indicatorNotes.in: the sailor lies 'in' the bunk as in a bed, so his letters go inside the word for bunk

blocks.note: bunk and rot both mean nonsense

annotation.surface: A sailor asleep in his bunk.
annotation.walkthrough: "Bunk" is a bed in the surface; here it means nonsense, ROT.
annotation.definitionFit: Said first of birds settling on a perch for the night, then loosely of people going to bed.

blocks.note: describes a timid person, apt to shrink from company

annotation.surface: An uncertain zone that is getting smaller.
annotation.walkthrough: "Grey area" reads as one phrase; the definition is only "Grey".
annotation.definitionFit: Ashy means ash-coloured, which is grey.

entries.clue: Plot to bring down most of factory (5,4)

indicatorNotes.most of: take all but the last letter of PLANT

blocks.note: to floor someone is to knock them down

annotation.surface: A conspiracy to demolish most of a factory.
annotation.walkthrough: "Plot" sounds like a scheme; it is a plan or diagram.
annotation.definitionFit: A plot can be a ground plan, and a floor plan is a drawing of a building's layout.

indicatorNotes.reflected: a mirror reflection reverses things, so the letters run backwards

annotation.surface: Someone in the dark contemplating their own reflection.
annotation.walkthrough: "Reflected" suits light bouncing off a mirror, but here it reverses both parts together, not just one.
annotation.definitionFit: Minus means without, as in 'minus his coat'.

blocks.note: a tick is a moment, as in 'just a tick'

annotation.surface: The pause in a comedian's act.
annotation.walkthrough: "Routine’s" looks possessive; the ’s is "is", linking definition to wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A Yiddish borrowing for the signature bit of business a performer repeats, which is a comedy routine.

indicatorNotes.flickering: flickering things move about unsteadily, so the letters shift

annotation.surface: People frightened of a flickering lamp.
annotation.walkthrough: "Flickering light" reads as one phrase; "flickering" works on the fodder and "light" means not heavy.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the weight sense: something with a feather's weightlessness is light, not the brightness sense the surface suggests.
